Explain the difference between point operations, linear filtering, and nonlinear filtering, giving an example of each.
risposta: A point operation computes each output pixel from only the corresponding input pixel, independent of neighbors (e.g. brightness g=f+b, contrast g=a*f, inversion 255-f, gamma correction). Linear filtering computes each output pixel as a weighted sum (convolution/cross-correlation) of a neighborhood using a kernel (e.g. box/mean filter, Gaussian blur, sharpening/unsharp masking). Nonlinear filtering also uses a neighborhood but the output is not a linear combination of neighbors (e.g. median filter for salt-and-pepper noise, bilateral filter for edge-preserving smoothing, thresholding).

domanda: Describe how histogram equalization works and what problem it solves.
risposta: Histogram equalization improves global contrast by redistributing intensity values to make the histogram flatter, so details become more visible. Steps: (1) compute the histogram p(rk)=#pixels with intensity rk over total pixels; (2) compute the cumulative distribution CDF(rk)=sum of p up to k; (3) use the scaled CDF as a lookup table to remap each old intensity to a new one (r'k=round((CDF-CDFmin)(L-1)/(N-CDFmin))). Local/adaptive HE (AHE) instead computes a transform per pixel from a local neighborhood to enhance local detail at higher computational cost.

domanda: Compare convolution and cross-correlation, and explain why convolution's properties are useful.
risposta: Both compute an output pixel as a weighted sum over a neighborhood with a kernel. Cross-correlation applies the kernel directly; convolution flips the kernel horizontally and vertically first. If the kernel is symmetric they are identical. Convolution is commutative, associative, and distributes over addition; cross-correlation lacks these. Associativity is especially useful: applying two filters in sequence equals convolving the kernels into one combined filter first, which also underlies the derivative theorem of convolution (differentiate the Gaussian once, then convolve).

domanda: Explain aliasing in image downsampling and how to prevent it, referencing the Nyquist criterion.
risposta: Naive sub-sampling (throwing away rows/columns) causes aliasing: fine details/patterns get distorted into incorrect new patterns because the sampling rate is too low to capture the highest frequencies. The Nyquist criterion requires fs >= 2*fmax. To prevent aliasing you first apply a low-pass filter (e.g. Gaussian blur) to remove high-frequency content that cannot be represented at the lower resolution, then sub-sample safely. This anti-aliasing step is also why Gaussian pyramids blur before downsampling.

domanda: Describe the full Canny edge detection pipeline and the role of each stage.
risposta: Canny is a multi-stage classical edge detector. (1) Filter: smooth with a Gaussian and compute gradient magnitude and orientation, e.g. with a Derivative-of-Gaussian or Sobel filter. (2) Non-maximum suppression: keep a pixel only if its magnitude is a local maximum along the gradient direction, otherwise set it to 0, producing thin single-pixel edges. (3) Hysteresis thresholding with two thresholds: pixels above the high threshold are strong edges and kept; pixels between low and high are weak edges, kept only if connected to a strong edge; pixels below the low threshold are discarded. This preserves true contours while removing noise.

domanda: Explain how image derivatives are used for edge detection and why Gaussian smoothing is combined with differentiation.
risposta: Edges are locations of rapid intensity change, so they are found via image derivatives. The gradient (df/dx, df/dy) points toward the steepest intensity increase; its magnitude measures edge strength and its orientation gives edge direction. Direct differentiation is very sensitive to noise (which creates many small rapid changes), so the image is first smoothed with a Gaussian. By the derivative theorem of convolution, smoothing and differentiation can be combined into a single Derivative-of-Gaussian (DoG) filter. Second-order methods use the Laplacian: edges appear as zero-crossings of a Laplacian-of-Gaussian (LoG), which localize edges more accurately though DoG is more efficient.
